newsitem.title: USA: U.S. nuclear waste policy wanted for Pena vote.
newsitem.headline: U.S. nuclear waste policy wanted for Pena vote.

text.p: The Senate Energy Committee chairman said in a letter released on Friday that he was delaying the energy secretary's confirmation because the White House has not offered a plan to store waste from nuclear power plants.
Alaska Republican Frank Murkowski was responding to a letter from committee Democrats who said they were fed up with delays in Federico Pena's confirmation.
Murkowski has twice canceled committee votes on Pena, and has not rescheduled a meeting for a vote that is necessary to send the nomination to the full Senate.

The Democrats said they were "dismayed" by Murkowski's linking of Pena's confirmation to getting White House concessions on a plan for storing radioactive waste from commercial reactors, and on making more timber available from a national forest in southeast Alaska.

Murkowski denied that Tongass National Forest timber issues have delayed the confirmation, saying he has been "quite careful in any meetings with the administration not to link any Alaska issues to the Pena nomination."

He said whether he will be able to work with Pena on the nuclear waste storage issue and whether the administration has a policy to deal with the problem "are legitimate and appropriate to pursue in the confirmation process."

But Democrats said the committee's consideration of Pena "should not depend upon the administration's views on these or other issues." They said Murkowski was making bipartisan cooperation on the committee "more difficult."

The federal government by law is to take responsibility by January 1998 of spent nuclear fuel accumulating at power plants across the country. But the administration has said it will not be able to do that because it has no place ready to store the waste. A site for long-term waste storage was not expected to be ready until well into the next century.
Murkowski pushed a bill to build a temporary waste repository in Nevada, near the only site under consideration for a permanent nuclear dump.

But President Clinton threatened to veto the bill, saying a temporary Nevada dump would compromise the study of whether to put a permanent repository there and that it would divert resources from building the permanent facility.
Nevada's two Democratic senators also vehemently oppose having a nuclear dump in their state.

The government has collected about $600 million a year since 1982 from utilities to build a waste dump, and Murkowski said it faces "substantial liability" starting next January for failing to take the waste off utilities' hands.

Murkowski said he has met with White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles this week in an effort to not delay Pena's confirmation process. But he said Bowles did not have a White House alternative on the nuclear issue, which Murkowksi found "unacceptable."
